**Multi-Source and Uncertainty-Aware Flash-Flood Prediction for Hilly Regions of India**&nbsp;

&nbsp;

**Problem Statement:** Develop and evaluate a multi-source, uncertainty-aware flash-flood early-warning model for hilly regions of India that fuses precipitation, soil moisture, terrain, hydrological conditions, and historical flood/landslide information. The study will quantify how additional data sources affect predictive performance, how missing or noisy observations propagate uncertainty into flood predictions, and how well the model generalizes across different locations and time periods. The final system will estimate flood probability, warning lead time, and prediction uncertainty and provide an interpretable risk level for decision support.&nbsp;

&nbsp;

**Regions:** 1st version \- Uttarakhand only. Then expand to sikkim and himachal pradesh

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

## **Models**&nbsp;

1. **Logistic Regression → Baseline model** — Very easy to train; gives interpretable flood probabilities and establishes a simple reference.  
2. **Random Forest → Non-linear baseline** — Very easy to train on our tabular environmental data; handles feature interactions well and requires little preprocessing.  
3. **XGBoost → Main prediction model** — Still easy to train with Scikit-learn-style code; likely to be our strongest tabular model and the main model used for deployment.  
4. **XGBoost \+ Conformal Prediction → Uncertainty-aware model** — Train XGBoost normally, then add conformal prediction to produce reliable prediction ranges/confidence; this is the main research component.  
5. **SHAP \+ Best Model → Interpretability layer** — Not a separate predictive model; explains which rainfall, soil, terrain and hydrological features influenced each prediction.

&nbsp;

**Research Flow**

1\. Multi-Source Data Fusion

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Determine the contribution of rainfall, soil, terrain,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;hydrology and historical hazard information.

&nbsp;

2\. Model Complexity Comparison

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost.

&nbsp;

3\. Observation Degradation

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Evaluate missing values, sensor outages and measurement noise.

&nbsp;

4\. Uncertainty Quantification

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Compare XGBoost with XGBoost \+ Conformal Prediction.

&nbsp;

5\. Spatial Generalization

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Train in one Himalayan region and test in another.

&nbsp;

6\. Temporal Generalization

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Train on earlier years and test on future years.

&nbsp;

7\. Feature Attribution

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Use SHAP to determine dominant predictors and their

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;stability across regions/seasons.

&nbsp;

8\. Warning Threshold Optimization

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Analyze false-alarm vs missed-flood trade-offs.

&nbsp;

9\. Warning Lead-Time Analysis

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Determine the useful prediction horizon.

&nbsp;

10\. Robustness × Uncertainty

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;→ Test whether uncertainty estimates remain trustworthy

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;as observation quality deteriorates.

&nbsp;

**Architecture**

![][image1]

![][image2]

Stages:&nbsp;  
**1\. Dataset Curation and Multi-Source Integration**

Curate and integrate heterogeneous datasets from **rainfall, soil moisture, river discharge, terrain, flood history, and landslide records** to create a unified, geographically and temporally aligned dataset for Uttarakhand flash-flood prediction.

### **2\. Data Transformation, Cleaning and Normalization**

Perform **data cleaning, missing-value handling, outlier detection, normalization, feature transformation, spatial-temporal alignment, and feature engineering** to convert raw multi-source data into a consistent ML-ready dataset.

### **3\. Optimized Multi-Model Training and Evaluation**

Develop and compare multiple ML models such as **Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost**, using **optimized training, hyperparameter tuning, efficient feature selection, and rigorous train/test validation** to identify reliable prediction models.

### **4\. Uncertainty-Aware and Robust Flood Prediction**

Enhance the selected model with **uncertainty estimation and robustness analysis**, evaluating prediction reliability under **missing, noisy, or degraded observations** and translating the results into practical early-warning levels.

**Research Papers:**&nbsp;

&nbsp;

## **1\. Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning Models for Flash Flood Prediction**

This paper studies how machine-learning-based flash-flood predictions are affected by uncertainty and noisy input observations. It is highly relevant to our uncertainty and observation-degradation experiments.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tgis.70254](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tgis.70254?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## **2\. A Deep Learning-Based Probabilistic Approach to Flash Flood Warnings in Mountainous Catchments**

This research develops probabilistic flash-flood warnings specifically for mountainous catchments. It studies the importance of antecedent precipitation and rainfall patterns in improving warning performance.

Full link:  
&nbsp;https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2025.132677

---

## **3\. Deep Learning Model for Flood Probabilistic Forecasting Considering Spatiotemporal Rainfall Distribution and Hydrologic Uncertainty**

This paper focuses on probabilistic flood forecasting by considering spatial and temporal rainfall patterns together with hydrological uncertainty. It is relevant to our multi-source data fusion and uncertainty-aware prediction approach.

Full link:  
&nbsp;https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2025.132879

---

## **4\. ML4FF: A Machine-Learning Framework for Flash Flood Forecasting Applied to a Brazilian Watershed**

This paper proposes a dedicated machine-learning framework for flash-flood forecasting and evaluates multiple ML approaches systematically. It is useful as a methodological reference for designing our model comparison and experimental framework.

Full link:  
&nbsp;https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2025.132674

---

## **5\. An Explainable Flash Flood Prediction Model in the Qinling Mountains**

This research focuses on flash-flood prediction in a mountainous environment and emphasizes explainability. It is particularly relevant to our use of SHAP and our focus on identifying the environmental factors responsible for warnings.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1111/jfr3.70136](https://doi.org/10.1111/jfr3.70136?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## **6\. Deep Learning for Cross-Region Streamflow and Flood Forecasting at a Global Scale**

This paper investigates whether deep-learning models can transfer knowledge across geographically different catchments. It strongly supports our proposed cross-region experiment between Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100617](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100617?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## **7\. Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning for Operational Flood Forecasting**

This research proposes a knowledge-guided machine-learning framework for operational flood forecasting using real-time precipitation, temperature and streamflow observations. It is useful for understanding how a research model can be designed for real-world forecasting systems.

Full link:  
&nbsp;https://doi.org/10.1029/2024WR039064

---

## **8\. Real Time Probabilistic Inundation Forecasts Using a LSTM Neural Network**

This paper develops real-time probabilistic flood inundation forecasts while considering uncertainty in rainfall predictions. It demonstrates how probabilistic outputs can improve the usefulness of flood early-warning systems.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2024.131082](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2024.131082?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## **9\. Comparison of Machine Learning Models for Flood Forecasting in the Mahanadi River Basin, India**

This India-focused research compares multiple machine-learning models for flood forecasting and investigates different input combinations. It is particularly useful for supporting our Random Forest and feature-ablation experiments.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.2166/wcc.2024.517](https://doi.org/10.2166/wcc.2024.517?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

---

## **10\. Enhancing Hydrological Extremes Forecasting Capabilities in Data-Scarce Regions Through Transfer Learning With Data Augmentation**

This paper addresses forecasting hydrological extremes in regions with limited observations using transfer learning and data augmentation. It is relevant to our research on data scarcity, missing observations and geographic generalization.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1029/2025EF006060](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025EF006060?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## **11\. Urban Flood Modeling and Forecasting With Deep Neural Operator and Transfer Learning**

This research investigates transfer learning and domain adaptation for flood forecasting across different scenarios. Although focused on urban flooding, it provides useful research ideas for our cross-region generalization experiments.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2025.133705](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2025.133705?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## **12\. Predicting Real-Time Roadway Pluvial Flood Risk: A Hybrid Machine Learning Approach Coupling a Graph-Based Flood Spreading Model, Historical Vulnerabilities, and Waze Data**

This paper combines multiple information sources, including historical vulnerability, physical flood modelling and real-time observations, to predict flood risk. It is a useful reference for our multi-source data-fusion architecture and real-time warning system.

Full link:  
&nbsp;[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2024.131406](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2024.131406?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
